title: Opening of the Western Wall Tunnel exit in Jerusalem's Old City (1996)
description: In September 1996, three months into his first term, Netanyahu and Jerusalem mayor Ehud Olmert decided to open an exit from the Western Wall Tunnel into the Muslim Quarter of the Old City, near the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound (the Temple Mount), a step Shimon Peres's government had put on hold. According to Britannica, the decision angered Palestinians and sparked intense fighting; Wikipedia's summary of the events reports three days of clashes in which dozens of Israelis and Palestinians were killed.
key_facts: September 1996: tunnel exit opened in the Muslim Quarter
Several days of deadly clashes followed (Britannica; Wikipedia)
Talks with Yasser Arafat resumed and led to the Hebron Protocol in January 1997

title: Prime Minister's Residence expenses and the conviction of Sara Netanyahu in the catering case
description: In 2015 reports surfaced that Sara Netanyahu, the prime minister's wife, had ordered meals from outside caterers at the state's expense although the residence employed a cook (nearly $100,000), and police recommended indicting her in 2016. Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit announced charges in September 2017 and she was indicted for fraud and breach of trust in 2018. On 16 June 2019 she signed a plea deal and was convicted of misusing state funds, the fraud charge being dropped, and was ordered to pay NIS 55,000 to the state. Benjamin Netanyahu was not a suspect or a party in the case.
key_facts: Netanyahu was not a party to the case
16 June 2019: Sara Netanyahu convicted under a plea deal of misusing state funds

title: Address to the US Congress against the Iran nuclear negotiations (2015)
description: On 3 March 2015, two weeks before an Israeli election, Netanyahu addressed a joint session of the US Congress to argue against the international negotiations with Iran that led to the 2015 nuclear agreement (JCPOA). The invitation had been issued by the Speaker of the House of Representatives without notifying the White House, a departure from protocol. According to Britannica, critics in Israel and the United States charged that by openly aligning himself with the partisan opponents of President Barack Obama he was putting bipartisan US support for Israel at risk; Netanyahu argued that any compromise would ultimately leave Iran with the option of developing nuclear weapons and that sanctions should be maintained.
key_facts: Invitation by the Speaker of the House without notifying the White House
Speech delivered on 3 March 2015; the JCPOA was concluded in July 2015

title: Election-day warning that ‘Arab voters are coming in droves’ (2015)
description: On election day, 17 March 2015, Netanyahu posted a video saying that ‘the rule of the right is in danger’ because ‘Arab voters are coming in droves to the ballot boxes’, bused in by left-wing NGOs. The remarks were condemned across the political spectrum, including by President Reuven Rivlin, and by the White House. On 23 March 2015 he apologised to Arab citizens, saying he had not meant to offend; the Joint List rejected the apology. The Attorney General's office later found that the remark did not amount to incitement to racism. In later campaigns Netanyahu said the remark had been twisted and that he had objected to support for the Joint List, not to Arab citizens voting.
key_facts: 17 March 2015: video warning of high Arab turnout
23 March 2015: apology to Arab citizens
Attorney General's office: no criminal incitement

title: Claim that the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem gave Hitler the idea of exterminating the Jews (2015)
description: In a speech to the World Zionist Congress in October 2015, Netanyahu said that in November 1941 the Palestinian Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, Haj Amin al-Husseini, told Hitler not to expel the Jews but to ‘burn them’. Historians including Yad Vashem's chief historian Dina Porat and Dan Michman of Bar-Ilan University and Yad Vashem said the claim was incorrect because the extermination had begun before the meeting; opposition leader Isaac Herzog accused him of trivialising the Holocaust and PLO official Saeb Erekat said the remarks absolved Hitler (The Guardian). Netanyahu said: ‘I didn't mean to absolve Hitler of responsibility, but to show that the father of the Palestinian nation wanted to destroy Jews even without occupation’, adding that Hitler ‘is responsible for the Final Solution’.
key_facts: October 2015 speech to the World Zionist Congress
Claim rejected by Holocaust historians

title: Brokering the 2019 electoral alliance of Jewish Home with the Kahanist Otzma Yehudit
description: Ahead of the April 2019 election Netanyahu pushed the Jewish Home party to run jointly with Otzma Yehudit, which the Times of Israel describes as the ideological heir of Rabbi Meir Kahane's Kach party, which was banned from the Knesset under a Basic Law provision against incitement and later outlawed in Israel, offering the merged list a slot on Likud's list and two cabinet posts so that right-wing votes would not be lost under the electoral threshold. The American Jewish Committee called Otzma Yehudit's views ‘reprehensible’ and AIPAC said it would not meet members of the ‘racist and reprehensible party’; opposition leaders including Yair Lapid accused Netanyahu of putting politics before the country. Netanyahu argued that if the smaller right-wing parties did not unite, some would fail to cross the electoral threshold, opening the way to a government of the left. Otzma Yehudit's leader Itamar Ben-Gvir became National Security Minister in Netanyahu's 2022 government.
key_facts: February 2019: merger deal midwifed by Netanyahu
AJC and AIPAC publicly condemn Otzma Yehudit
2022: Ben-Gvir appointed National Security Minister

title: Policy towards Hamas before 7 October 2023, including Qatari cash transfers to Gaza
description: For years before the war Netanyahu's governments allowed Qatar to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars into the Hamas-run Gaza Strip, which Netanyahu publicly defended as necessary to prevent a humanitarian collapse. After the 7 October 2023 attack, critics, including Times of Israel political correspondent Tal Schneider in an analysis, argued that his governments had divided power between Gaza and the West Bank, weakening Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas while tolerating and strengthening Hamas in order to forestall a Palestinian state. The Times of Israel noted in 2026 that, despite vowing in the 2009 campaign to topple Hamas, he avoided destabilising its rule over the following 14 years. Netanyahu has defended his record, including in an August 2024 interview with Time magazine in which he defended allowing financial support for Gaza's Hamas-run administration.
key_facts: Before October 2023: Qatari funds enter Gaza with Israeli approval
8 October 2023: Times of Israel analysis on the policy of ‘propping up’ Hamas
August 2024: Netanyahu defends allowing financial support for Gaza's Hamas-run administration

title: Judicial overhaul, mass protests and the first dismissal of Defence Minister Gallant (2023)
description: The judicial overhaul announced by Justice Minister Yariv Levin in January 2023 with Netanyahu's backing triggered what the Times of Israel describes as a protest movement unparalleled in Israel's history, with weekly demonstrations of hundreds of thousands and refusals of reserve duty. Critics argued it would remove the main checks on government power, and pointed to Netanyahu's ongoing trial; Netanyahu and Levin said it would restore balance between the branches. On 26 March 2023, after Defence Minister Yoav Gallant publicly called for a pause for security reasons, Netanyahu announced his dismissal (later reversed), prompting mass protests and the threat of a nationwide strike; he then froze the legislation. The reasonableness amendment passed in July 2023 was annulled by the High Court in January 2024.
key_facts: 4 January 2023: Levin's plan presented
26 March 2023: Netanyahu announces Gallant's dismissal; reversed in April
March 2023: legislation frozen; July 2023: reasonableness law passed; January 2024: annulled

title: Responsibility for the 7 October 2023 failures and refusal of a state commission of inquiry
description: The Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage according to Israeli figures, was the deadliest day in Israel's history and was widely described as the country's worst intelligence and security failure. Several senior security officials said they took responsibility; Netanyahu said ‘everyone will have to give answers … including me’ after the war, but, according to the Times of Israel, he has never explicitly accepted responsibility and has blamed the security services, previous governments, the judiciary and political opponents. He opposes a state commission of inquiry, whose members would be chosen by the Supreme Court president, saying it would be biased against him; his coalition instead backed a politically appointed commission whose scope, he said, should include the Oslo Accords, the 2005 Gaza disengagement and the 2023 protest movement. Polls cited by the Times of Israel show a majority of Israelis favour a state commission. In July 2026 the government told the High Court there would be no inquiry before the election.
key_facts: 25 October 2023: ‘everyone will have to give answers … including me … only after the war’
Bill for a politically appointed inquiry passed only a first reading (59–0), boycotted by the opposition
22 July 2026: government asks the High Court not to intervene before the election

title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza: aid restrictions, casualty toll and the 2025 famine determination
description: The conduct of the war in Gaza under Netanyahu's government drew international criticism over the civilian toll and restrictions on humanitarian aid. According to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is run by Hamas and does not distinguish civilians from combatants, 74,377 people had been killed in the Strip by 11 October 2026, including 1,488 since the October 2025 ceasefire; in January 2026 a senior Israeli military official said the army believed the toll of about 70,000 to be largely accurate, with the civilian–combatant breakdown still under review. Israel imposed an 11-week blockade on aid after the ceasefire collapsed in March 2025; in August 2025 the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) declared famine in parts of the Strip, estimating that 514,000 people were experiencing famine. Netanyahu's office called the declaration an ‘outright lie’ and a ‘modern blood libel’, saying ‘Israel does not have a policy of starvation’ and blaming shortages on Hamas's theft of aid; Israel's Foreign Ministry accused the IPC of lowering its own thresholds; the IPC said it had used a measurement easier to track in wartime. As of October 2026 the IPC still projected severe hunger for most of Gaza's population (Al Jazeera). The ICC arrest warrant against Netanyahu (see justice) concerns alleged starvation as a method of warfare, which he denies.
key_facts: Gaza Health Ministry toll: 74,377 killed by 11 October 2026 (figures do not separate combatants)
January 2026: senior IDF official says the ministry's overall toll of about 70,000 is largely accurate
August 2025: IPC famine determination; Netanyahu's office calls it a ‘modern blood libel’

title: South Africa v. Israel genocide case at the International Court of Justice
description: In December 2023 South Africa brought a case against the State of Israel before the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention, accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza; Israel rejects the accusation as false and antisemitic. The case is against the state, not against Netanyahu personally, who is not a party to it; it concerns the conduct of the war waged by his government. The Court ordered provisional measures in 2024. Several states have intervened, including Türkiye; in March 2026 the United States, Hungary, Namibia, Fiji, the Netherlands and Iceland filed declarations of intervention, and in September 2026 Colombia withdrew its declaration.
key_facts: Case against the State of Israel; Netanyahu is not a party
As of September 2026: written stage, with time-limits fixed for a Reply and a Rejoinder

title: Support for the US proposal to relocate Gaza's population (‘voluntary emigration’, 2025)
description: After US President Donald Trump proposed in February 2025 that the United States take over the Gaza Strip and that its residents be relocated to other countries, Netanyahu said he was ‘committed to President Trump's plan for the creation of a different Gaza’ and described departures as voluntary; Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered the army to prepare a plan for Gazans to leave ‘voluntarily’. A UN spokesperson said the UN would oppose any plan leading to the forced displacement of people or ‘any type of ethnic cleansing’, and Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the Palestinian Authority and the Arab League rejected the transfer of Palestinians from Gaza ‘under any circumstances’. The September 2025 US 20-point plan accepted by Netanyahu states that ‘no one will be forced to leave Gaza’ and that those who leave will be free to return.
key_facts: 17 February 2025: Netanyahu says Israel is committed to Trump's plan
Arab states and the UN reject any forced displacement
September 2025: the 20-point plan provides that Gazans will not be forced to leave

title: Leak of a classified Hamas document to Bild by aides in the Prime Minister's Office (2024)
description: In September 2024, days after six hostages were killed in captivity in Rafah and amid mass protests over a hostage deal, a nine-month-old internal Hamas memo obtained by military intelligence and blocked by the military censor was published by the German daily Bild, apparently to support Netanyahu's argument that Hamas, not he, was blocking a deal; media later reported that Bild had distorted the document. Eli Feldstein, Netanyahu's spokesman on military affairs, and reservist Ari Rosenfeld were indicted, and on 11 June 2026 his senior media adviser Jonatan Urich was indicted for transmitting classified information with intent to harm state security and for destroying evidence. In December 2025 Feldstein told the Kan broadcaster that Netanyahu was ‘behind’ the leak and had agreed with him and Urich to say falsely that he had learned of the document from the media; Likud downplayed Netanyahu's ties to Feldstein and called the affair a distraction. According to the Times of Israel, Netanyahu himself is not a suspect in the case.
key_facts: Netanyahu is not a suspect or defendant
Defendants: Eli Feldstein, Ari Rosenfeld and, since June 2026, Jonatan Urich (Tel Aviv District Court)
None of the defendants had been convicted as of October 2026

title: ‘Qatargate’: investigation of Netanyahu aides over alleged paid pro-Qatar messaging
description: Since March 2025 police and the Shin Bet have investigated suspicions that Netanyahu's aides Jonatan Urich and Eli Feldstein, while working for the prime minister, were paid to promote pro-Qatari messages to journalists in order to burnish Qatar's image as a mediator in the hostage talks; suspected offences include contact with a foreign agent, bribery, fraud, breach of trust and money laundering. A third adviser, Yisrael Einhorn, lives in Serbia and was questioned there. In August 2026 Channel 13 reported that the attorney general was expected to decide to charge Urich and Feldstein with security offences, and a former senior Mossad official pending a hearing. The affair also figured in Netanyahu's attempt to dismiss Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who said his dismissal was linked to the investigation. Netanyahu is not a suspect; Likud denied that he served Qatari interests and called the case ‘fake’, and Feldstein denied knowingly working for Qatar.
key_facts: Netanyahu is not a suspect; his aides are
March 2025: Urich and Feldstein arrested and questioned
August 2026: charges reported to be expected, pending decisions by the attorney general

title: Dismissals of Defence Minister Gallant, Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara
description: On 5 November 2024 Netanyahu dismissed Defence Minister Yoav Gallant, saying that ‘trust between me and the defence minister was damaged’; according to The Guardian, the two had clashed over war strategy and how to bring the hostages home, and Gallant had just renewed efforts to enforce conscription of ultra-Orthodox men. Protests broke out across Israel. In March 2025 the cabinet voted to dismiss Shin Bet director Ronen Bar, who said the move was linked to the agency's investigations of the Prime Minister's Office; on 21 May 2025 the High Court ruled that the dismissal was unlawful and that Netanyahu had a conflict of interest, though it issued no orders because Bar had announced his resignation; Netanyahu called the ruling ‘disgraceful’ and ‘puzzling’. In 2025 the government also voted to dismiss Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara; on 14 December 2025 the High Court unanimously annulled the dismissal, and several ministers urged the government to defy the ruling. In July 2026 the coalition passed a law curtailing the attorney general's powers.
key_facts: 5 November 2024: Gallant dismissed; replaced by Israel Katz
21 May 2025: High Court rules Bar's dismissal unlawful, citing Netanyahu's conflict of interest
14 December 2025: High Court annuls the attorney general's dismissal (7–0)

title: Reports that Netanyahu received warnings from Arab leaders before 7 October 2023 (2026)
description: On 8 September 2026 Haaretz reported, citing unnamed sources, that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu in a phone call about ten days before 7 October 2023 that Yahya Sinwar was preparing a ‘huge surprise’ and had earlier passed the message to the Shin Bet, and that Netanyahu did not relay it to the security chiefs; Ynet, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported a separate warning by Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel. Netanyahu called the Haaretz report ‘fabricated’ and ‘false’, and his lawsuit states that official Prime Minister's Office records contain no record of contact with bin Zayed between 1 September and 7 October 2023. The UAE initially declined to comment; an Emirati official later denied that bin Zayed had personally warned Netanyahu of an imminent attack, while Israeli media cited a New York Times report in which five Israeli officials supported the account. Haaretz said it stood by its investigation. Netanyahu sued the outlets and journalists for defamation (see justice).
key_facts: 8 September 2026: Haaretz report based on unnamed sources
Netanyahu denies receiving the warnings
29 September 2026: defamation suit filed in the Jerusalem District Court

title: Media overhaul law and Netanyahu's conflict-of-interest arrangement (2026)
description: On 16–17 July 2026 the Knesset passed Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi's media overhaul 53–48, expanding government influence over broadcast regulation, ratings and state advertising and, according to the Times of Israel, including benefits for the pro-government Channel 14. Netanyahu, whose criminal trial concerns alleged attempts to obtain favourable media coverage, took part in the debate but not the vote; Karhi thanked him from the podium for giving him ‘the mission… to deliver right-wing reform of the media’ four years earlier. The Times of Israel wrote that such a directive would appear to violate the conflict-of-interest arrangement Netanyahu signed with the attorney general barring him from media policy; Karhi said he had a legal opinion that Netanyahu was not in a conflict of interest. Watchdog groups and parties petitioned the High Court against the law, citing procedural flaws.
key_facts: 17 July 2026: media law passed 53–48 hours before the Knesset dispersed
Karhi: the reform was a mission given by Netanyahu
Petitions pending before the High Court
